papers.title: Error correction on an array of superconducting qubits with defective components
papers.abstract: A solid-state quantum-computing architecture will require the fabrication of arrays of many coupled qubits. It is inevitable that this process will produce qubits and couplers with varying performance, with some components underperforming due to imperfect fabrication. Quantum error-correction requires high-performing components and hence these defects must be dealt with, either by adapting the code to exclude the defects, or by informing the decoder to accommodate defects in post-processing. Here we implement and compare strategies to operate distance-5 surface codes on a quantum processor consisting of a square-lattice array of 120 superconducting qubits. We demonstrate a dramatic reduction in the probability of a logical error in a memory experiment by excluding underperforming components, compared with both a standard approach of ignoring defects, and a defect-aware decoding approach. We observe up to 2.8X improvement in logical errors per round when excluding defects compared with the standard defect-ignorant approach (1.62% compared to 4.49%). In contrast, defect-aware decoding gives only modest gains. Defects are also expected to be particularly harmful for measurement-based logical operations. Using a stability experiment we show that excluding defects resurrects measurement-based logic gate performance, observing a 6.3% per-round suppression of failure rate when excluding defects, compared to zero suppression otherwise. Furthermore, we show a further substantial decrease in logical errors when using leakage post-selection in combination with our defect exclusion strategies, resulting in a distance-5 code outperforming the best distance-3 in one basis. Our experiments therefore give a proof-of-principle demonstration of the essential utility of defect exclusion methods in the scale-up of solid-state quantum computing approaches.

Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit

summary.summary: This work demonstrates distance-5 surface codes on the 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk processor with active defect exclusion strategies that quarantine underperforming qubits and couplers. Combining defect exclusion with noise-informed decoding and leakage post-selection yields a distance-5 code outperforming the best distance-3 instance in one basis.
summary.motivation: Fabrication of larger superconducting qubit arrays inevitably produces components with varying performance; defects must be mitigated either through decoder adaptation or active circuit modification to achieve practical quantum error correction.
summary.method: Distance-5 surface codes were implemented using super-stabilizer constructions and ancilla repurposing to avoid defects identified by benchmark (coupler error rate >5%, measure-qubit error >$7\times10^{-2}$, data-qubit $T_1$ or $T_2$ <80 µs). Performance was evaluated via memory experiments (logical error per round vs syndrome rounds) and stability experiments (failure rate decay with measurement rounds) with BeliefMatching decoding informed by calibration data.
summary.result: Defect exclusion reduced logical error per round from 4.49% to 1.62% in Pauli-Z basis (2.8× improvement) for memory, and restored measurement-based gate suppression in stability experiments ($\Gamma=0.94$ vs $\Gamma\geq1$ without exclusion). With leakage post-selection (3% cutoff), distance-5 achieved 0.98% error per round versus 1.26% for distance-3.

papers.title: Systematic modulation of superconducting gap dynamics in YBCO|BNT|YBCO Josephson Junctions through THz field interaction and BNT ferroelectric barrier
papers.abstract: The integration of ferroelectric barriers into high-temperature Josephson junctions offers a pathway to tunable superconducting quantum devices. Here, we demonstrate robust Josephson coupling in YBa2Cu3O7-x (YBCO)/Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3 (BNT)/YBCO trilayer junctions incorporating a 40 nm ferroelectric BNT barrier. Epitaxial trilayers were fabricated by pulsed laser deposition on SrTiO3 substrates and investigated under broadband terahertz (THz) irradiation (0.5-2.5 THz). At 1.5 THz, close to the Josephson plasma resonance, the BNT polarization increased from 33.4 to 46.4 uC/cm2 at 30 K, enhancing superconducting transport. The junctions exhibited a well-defined zero-voltage supercurrent branch, with the critical current Ic(T) remaining nearly constant up to 60 K and reaching 468.2 uA under 1.5 THz excitation, evidencing strong phase coherence. Scanning tunneling spectroscopy revealed an enhanced superconducting gap in YBCO/BNT/YBCO (Delta = 1.3 meV) compared with pure YBCO (Delta = 1.05 meV), while optical conductivity measurements showed a reduction in conductivity and gap with increasing temperature, consistent with BCS theory under THz excitation. Atomic force microscopy and X-ray reflectivity confirmed uniform morphology and sharp interfaces, excluding defect-mediated transport. Magnetic field modulation of Ic(B) exhibited a canonical Fraunhofer interference pattern, and resistance mapping revealed alternating lobes of high and low dissipation, indicating coherent Josephson tunneling. These results establish that Josephson coupling is intrinsic to the YBCO/BNT/YBCO junctions, enabled by the dipolar character and dynamic THz response of the BNT barrier. This study identifies BNT as a viable, tunable barrier material for next-generation high-Tc superconducting quantum devices.

summary.summary: YBCO/BNT/YBCO Josephson junctions with a 40 nm ferroelectric BNT barrier show robust superconducting coupling and tunable transport under THz excitation at 0.5–2.5 THz. At 1.5 THz near the plasma resonance, the junctions exhibit a critical current of 468.2 µA with an enhanced superconducting gap ($\Delta = 1.3$ meV) and stable $I_c(T)$ up to 60 K, with BNT polarization increasing from 33.4 to 46.4 µC/cm$^2$ at 30 K.
summary.motivation: Ferroelectric barriers in high-$T_c$ Josephson junctions offer dynamic tuning through polarization control, enabling the design of reconfigurable quantum devices beyond conventional fixed-barrier architectures.
summary.method: YBCO/BNT/YBCO trilayers were grown by pulsed laser deposition on SrTiO$_3$ substrates and characterized under broadband THz irradiation (0.5–2.5 THz) using scanning tunneling spectroscopy, optical conductivity, magnetic field modulation, and structural techniques (AFM, X-ray reflectivity).
summary.result: At 1.5 THz resonance, the junction achieves $I_c = 468.2$ µA with canonical Fraunhofer diffraction and zero-field supercurrent branch; the superconducting gap increases to 1.3 meV (24% enhancement over bare YBCO), and $I_c(T)$ remains nearly flat to 60 K, confirming intrinsic coherent Josephson tunneling mediated by the ferroelectric barrier.

papers.title: A cryogenic neutral-atom platform with full optical access and 2-hour trap lifetime
papers.abstract: Neutral-atom quantum processors are rapidly scaling toward system sizes of more than ten thousand qubits, allowing for the realization of a new class of quantum computing algorithms and quantum simulation experiments. However, current neutral-atom platforms generally have to find a compromise between the optical accessibility and the storage time of atoms in optical potentials, limiting the available qubit numbers. Here we report on the operation of a novel, cryogenically enhanced, neutral-atom apparatus that overcomes these apparently conflicting requirements. We demonstrate vacuum-limited trapping lifetimes of up to two hours of single $^{88}\mathrm{Sr}$ atoms in an optical tweezer array while preserving full optical access and without the need for complex cryogenic enclosures. Our measurements show that exceptionally long single-atom lifetimes can be achieved with a relatively simple cryostat design. Our architecture can be straightforwardly ported to other atomic species and shows a viable path for scaling up to sorted arrays of tens of thousands of atoms.

similar_to.title: Quantum-limited millimeter wave to optical transduction
Demonstrating Quantum Error Correction that Extends the Lifetime of Quantum Information

summary.summary: This work demonstrates vacuum-limited trapping lifetimes exceeding 7000 s (∼2 hours) for single $^{88}$Sr atoms in optical tweezers using a simple cryogenic design with a 4 K cold tip, while maintaining full optical access without complex in-vacuum windows. The apparatus achieves high vacuum pressure ($\sim 2.5 \times 10^{-12}$ mbar) through material selection (grade 2 titanium), bakeout procedures, and hydrogen cryopumping, without the thermal load constraints that limit scaling in conventional 4 K platforms.
summary.motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are scaling toward 10,000+ qubits, but existing platforms face a tradeoff between optical accessibility and atom storage lifetime due to background gas collisions and the complexity of cryogenic enclosures that restrict optical access. Extending trapping lifetimes while preserving optical access is essential for sorting large defect-free arrays and enabling scaled quantum processors.
summary.method: A bakeable UHV chamber constructed primarily from grade 2 titanium (superior hydrogen outgassing characteristics) was coupled to a commercial closed-cycle cryostat (ColdEdge Stinger) cooling a cold tip to 4 K approximately 30 cm from the tweezer array. Single $^{88}$Sr atoms in a $16 \times 16$ optical tweezer array (spacing 4 µm, depth ∼220 µK) were held under various cooling protocols (continuous/pulsed Sisyphus cooling, pulsed sideband cooling) to measure survival probability versus hold time and distinguish loss mechanisms.
summary.result: With pulsed Sisyphus and sideband cooling, lifetimes exceed 7000 s; without cooling, lifetimes reach several hundred seconds even at room temperature. Deliberately heating the cold tip to 30 K induces a pressure spike from hydrogen desorption, confirming the cold tip acts as a cryopump. Lifetime increases monotonically with tweezer trap depth and decreases with oven temperature, while remaining independent of tweezer optical power (up to the tested range), demonstrating compatibility with scaling to large arrays without thermal load degradation of the cryogenic system.

papers.title: Traceable In Situ Microwave Power Measurement at the Cryogenic Device Plane in a Dilution Refrigerator
papers.abstract: Accurate knowledge of the microwave power delivered to a cryogenic device under test (DUT) is essential for the characterization and operation of superconducting quantum circuits. However, this information is difficult to obtain inside dilution refrigerators because of distributed attenuation, impedance mismatch, switch-path repeatability, and temperature-dependent microwave components. This paper presents an in situ measurement method for RF power at the cryogenic device plane. The method uses a custom variable temperature stage (VTS) as a cryogenic thermal-transfer element. The TVS is alternately heated by a four-wire DC heater and by microwave power dissipated in a 20 dB pass-through attenuator. By fitting the thermal transients and comparing the corresponding steady-state temperatures, the absorbed microwave power is inferred from a directly measured DC electrical power through an AC/DC substitution procedure. The finite reflection and transmission of the attenuator are then accounted for by cryogenic two-port scattering-parameter measurements based on a switch-assisted Short--Open--Load--Reciprocal calibration, so that the result is referred to the DUT reference plane. The system is demonstrated in a dilution refrigerator with powers between -43 and -58 dBm at the DUT input plane. The demonstrated relative standard uncertainty ranges from about 2% at -43.9 dBm to about 40% at -57.6 dBm. The proposed approach combines thermal RF power transfer, cryogenic S-parameter correction, and uncertainty evaluation in a measurement architecture compatible with quantum-device experiments, providing a practical route toward traceable microwave-power calibration at millikelvin stages.

A Modular Cryogenic Link for Microwave Quantum Communication Over Distances of Tens of Meters

summary.summary: This work presents a traceable in situ microwave power measurement method for superconducting quantum circuits in dilution refrigerators using AC/DC thermal substitution with a custom variable temperature stage (VTS). The method combines cryogenic calorimetry with SOLR scattering-parameter calibration to measure incident RF power at the device reference plane, demonstrating measurements from $-43$ to $-58$ dBm with relative uncertainties ranging from 2% to 40%.
summary.motivation: Accurate knowledge of microwave power delivered to cryogenic quantum devices is essential for precise circuit-QED characterization and device operation, yet this is difficult to obtain inside dilution refrigerators due to distributed cable attenuation, temperature-dependent component behavior, and impedance mismatches between room temperature and the millikelvin stage.
summary.method: A macroscopic OFHC copper VTS thermally weakly coupled to the dilution refrigerator's cold finger ($\sim 80$ mK) is alternately heated by DC (four-wire resistor) and RF (20 dB pass-through attenuator) while measuring temperature transients via RuOx thermometry. Steady-state temperatures are fit with a thermal model to perform AC/DC power substitution, then corrected via cryogenic SOLR calibration of the attenuator's scattering parameters ($|S_{11}|$, $|S_{21}|$) to refer the result to the DUT plane.
summary.result: RF power measurements between $-43.87$ dBm (40.9 nW, 2% uncertainty) and $-57.58$ dBm (1.74 nW, 40% uncertainty) at 4 GHz, with dominant uncertainty contributions from parasitic heating fluctuations ($P_0$) and VTS steady-state temperature extraction; lower-power sensitivity is limited by signal indistinguishability from the $\sim 91$ nW background power.
